texto: This movie is a genuine embarrassment in everyway imaginable, but there's one thing that bothers me more than anything else. That being you can truly feel the utter disdain Marvel has for both Black Widow and Captain Marvel. This movie is supposed to be a "celebration" of the mcu and it's history with non-stop nostalgia bait and a constant self congratulatory tone all throughout. It gives big moments for every single character no matter how minor they are, except for those two. Instead they use what little time they give Black Widow and Captain Marvel to humiliate and degrade them every second they're on screen. They setup Captain Marvel at the end of Infinity War only to throw her away as soon as this movie begins. They kill off Black Widow and every character immediately moves on without any care only to have the entire last act of the movie be about honoring Iron Man and showing his death massively impacting everyone's lives. There's more to this, but I don't feel like getting into it. I despise this movie.

As the end marker for a long running generation of marvel movies, Endgame unfortunately drops the ball in all ways that matter. A lame attempt at reconciling irreversible character and wider plot choices, this film not only disrupts long established character growth and progression, but it also abruptly cuts off any opportunity for what many would call a “happy ending.” Multiple beloved characters are given the “tortured male existence trope,” wherein their wider personality and moral identity are swept to the wayside in order to justify a new generation of characters to swoop in following their exit. For example, by both butchering Peggy Carter and Steve Rogers emotional maturation and individuality in order to manufacture a “romantic reunification” following Steve’s travel back in time, Marvel has essentially removed both Peggy’s autonomy outside of being “Captain Americas love interest,” as well as Steve’s long established faithfulness to Bucky Barnes and his dedication to serving the weak. In no world would Steve rogers abandon a freshly reintroduced to society Bucky, nor a disrupted world reeling with the sudden re-appearance of 50% of the world’s population. In his decision to abandon his shield and interrupt Peggy’s progression towards an accomplished life as a shield founder and agent, as well as her pursuit of future love and motherhood as expressed in the original timeline, Steve is making an exceptionally selfish decision—which as any Marvel fan is aware—is the antithesis of his character. This is just one of the irreconcilable changes made to a central character that insults years of character establishment and development, which is then followed by yet again a female character being fridged for the greater plot. First starting with Gamora in Infinity war and now Natasha in Endgame, it is clear to see that the writers find no use for these strong female characters in these last plot stages other than as a motivation for male suffering and lament. Gamora, both present and past iterations of herself (as featured in this film), have much more worth as a character representing long building abusive deprogramming and female strength and endurance in the face of tragedy, than as a “sad she’s different than my girlfriend” trope—as presented by Peter Quills reaction to her appearance. Prior to this, viewers are slapped in the face with the sacrifice of Natasha for the soul stone, where her death is framed as a noble sacrifice in order to allow Clint Barton to return to his family once the snap is reversed. While faithful to Natasha’s character, one can only reconcile so much with the fact that it had to be only female character of the original Avengers to lose her life first. This is especially exasperated by the emphasized female power scene in the final battle, where every female hero on scene band together to fight, almost as an attempt by the writers to apologize for killing off the woman who pioneered female superhero-dom in modern media not 40 minutes earlier. All in all, these are just some of the many faults within this movie—which in its essence is a blatant attempt to slap a crooked bandaid on Marvels obvious (and clumsy) transition to a newer generation of actors and characters. As entertaining as a battle packed, time travel action movie can be, Avengers Endgame is a lazy attempt at hopefully pushing viewers towards future projects as they kill off their favorite characters one by one. We can only hope that these new superhero’s will be given the opportunity to grow into characters of their own and establish a storyline outside of the shadow of their predecessors.

There are so many things wrong with this movie that I don't know where to start. Visually, for starters, it's ugly, with its dull, colorless imagery and lifeless lighting. The VFX are decent for the movie's budget—they're not mind-blowing or incredible. That said, a lot of the green-screen shots are pretty obvious and look terrible. As for the plot, it’s pretty embarrassing. Between its desire to lecture other time-travel movies (even though it can’t even stick to its own ridiculous concept), its inability to acknowledge that Thanos’s motivations were understandable but morally wrong, and its characters who all act out of sheer selfishness or guilt, like Captain America, who casually mentions that whales have returned to the Hudson because of less pollution and fewer boats, but who ultimately doesn’t care and just wants to bring everyone back... Or the fact that he stays in the past to live with Carter, changing the timeline in the process since she had normally remarried. The only two characters who behave normally are Barton, who seeks nothing more than to kill criminals, as if trying to restore some kind of balance; and Carol Danvers, who reminds us quite often throughout the film that Earth isn't the center of the universe, something even a character like Rocket seems to forget. 3 hours and 20 minutes of demagoguery, cynicism, and selfishness that turn these superheroes into some real jerks.

It felt like a massive letdown after Infinity War, the pacing feels oddly slow, the action is underwhelming, Thanos gets defeated way too easily and way too fast after the menace that he was in Infinity war, there are plenty of ass pulls and conveniences like Cap being able to use Mjolnir and how they collect the Stones, the entire first third of the movie about time travel makes no sense at all, there is way too much fanservice, throwbacks to previous Marvel movies like the elevator Captain America scene, the Ancient One hands over the Time Stone way too easily, the Aether was notoriously hard to extract in Dark World but now Rocket does it easily offscreen. What's done to Thor is downright horrendous, there was a lot of potential with him falling into deep depression, but it just turns into fat and beer jokes mocking a broken man, and nothing deeper than that. Also same thing with Hulk, why did he off screen somehow manage to control and get along with Hulk and become one somehow? When that was such an issue all the time and especially in Infinity War. Also how come when the Ancient One snaps him out of his body, it's just Banner? Not Hulk and Banner or "Professor Hulk" at least? Also Steve chooses to live his life out with Carter in the past, but abandons Bucky? The same Cap who risked it all for him in Winter Soldier and Civil War now chooses to ignore all of that and leave his best friend? I wish we got to see more of the world after half the population got decimated but it's quickly forgotten. It's pure spectacle over substance and you don't see any progression in character arcs, you only skip to their climax, Thor, Tony, Hulk, Cap, Clint, they are wildly different after the time skip but you don't see any of it, it would've been better if there was 3 or 4 more movies before Endgame after Infinity War, it's clear it was rushed and the movie dragged a lot.

Ouais. Ok. Cool. Franchement ce film a cette note car c'est un film charnière, sinon je lui aurais mis 2 étoiles en terme de kiffe. Je n'ai ressenti aucune émotions, cela ne m'a pas fait rire et je n'étais pas ébahi ni ému. Le début est sympathique, voir Thor gros alcoolo c'est étrange, de même voir Tony Stark avec un enfant m'a surpris, mais c'est tout. Déjà je n'apprécie pas le fait de remonter le temps à l'aide de la technologique quantique. Ensuite je ne pense pas que les pierres permettent de refermer la branche d'univers créée (donc il existe trois univers distincts, le premier est celui dans lequel l'histoire se passe, le second est celui dans lequel on a prit les pierres et le dernier est celui dans lequel on a pris les pierres puis on les a restitués). Enfin Steve Rogers devrait avoir plus de 100 ans donc comment est-il en vie à la fin pour transmettre le costume et le bouclier ?? Cela étant dit c'était sympathique de revenir dans les précédents films, mais bon moi ce ne m'a pas trop touché vu que je les ai vu pour la plupart il y a moins de dix jours. Captain America est symbole et non un super-héros classique, il représente l'Amérique mais aussi la loyauté, le courage, le charisme, il est donc impersonnel et tout le monde qui est en digne peut être Captain America, c'est pour cela que je ne suis pas gêné par le fait que Steve Rogers ne soit plus Captain America à présent. D'ailleurs en parlant de dignité, j'ai trouve ça hyper classe que Steve Rogers ait pu maîtriser Mjöllnir. J'ai trop le seum que Black Widow soit morte c'est une de mes préférées. Elle aurait dû être présente pour l'une des meilleurs scènes du film : Toutes les super-héroïnes combattant côte à côte. La scène du sacrifice entre Hawkeye et Black Widow est bien je trouve et aussi un peu émouvante. Je suis pas content que Captain Marvel n'ait pas fait grand chose, je pense qu'elle peut prendre Thanos en 1v1 facile et c'est bien la seule. Dans mon classement elle est deuxième devant Wanda et derrière Doctor Strange. J'ai bien aimé aussi que l'Ancien soit présente pour défendre la Terre lorsque Loki était de mèche avec Ronan. J'apprécie le geste héroïque de Tony Stark qui fait subir à Thanos ce qu'il a fait subir à la moitié des êtres vivants. J'aime bien quand Thor et Peter se lancent dans une guerre d'egros (parce qu'ils ont tous les deux un énorme ego et qu'ils sont gros, hehehehehehehe je suis très fier et je souris bêtement derrière l'écran). Il y a une dernière question que je me pose du coup, dans l'histoire on est en 2019 ou bien 2024, ceux qui sont restés vivants ont vieillis par conséquent tous les élèves du lycée de Peter Parker sont morts parce que sinon certains auraient fini leurs études. Bon on verra bien parce que j'ai pas vu Spider-Man : Far from Home. Papa a répondu à une des mes contestations Captain America est encore vivant car il n'est plus un homme normal (ça fait sens). Bref le film ne m'a pas enthousiasmé. Après avoir réfléchi durant la nuit je compte au moins 9 univers parallèle, l'originel puis 4 paires d'univers (car les pierres ont été empruntés à des années différentes) constitué de la manière suivante : un univers dans lequel la pierre n'est plus puis un autre où la pierre n'était plus avant qu'elle ne soit restituée. Mais du coup ces univers dans lesquels rien ne semble avoir changer possède le même futur que l'original et du coup cela créer infiniment des univers parallèles. Donc maintenant on ne sait pas si nous sommes dans l'univers originel ou dans une des répliques (peut-être que je me trompe et qu'il y a une faille dans mon raisonnement). Du coup même si Rogers avait la capacité de vivre plus de 100 ans, il ne devrait pas être dans cette timeline et n'aurait pas donc pu transmettre son rôle. Vu le 06/08/2026

I think this more negative approach I'm having with this rewatch stems from the anxiety of the upcoming Avengers movie being centered around my favorite comic book character of all time, Dr Doom, who is miles more powerful and methodical than a character like Thanos. As well as the MCU's portrayal of the character was, Thanos could and should never hold a candle. Before the MCU was celebrated for giving a new life and dedicated following to all the B-list characters Marvel had to settle with due to the big 3 (Spider-Man, F4, and the X-Men) being owned by Fox and Sony, there was a legacy of iconic comic heroes and villains that spanned over half a decade. And within the culture of comics, if you asked someone to name a comic book villain from Marvel Comics, 9/10 you're not going to hear Thanos, Ultron, or even Venom. They will say Dr. Doom. To the comic fan, Thanos is a nice can of RC Cola, but Doom... Doom is Coke from a glass. Despite this level of hype this character is known for, his film adaptations have been genuinely terrible, to the point of being disrespectful (I'm looking at you F4 2016). I guess the point I'm trying to make is that the luster is being lost for me in this film, along with the decisions of the past and present, which make me enjoy this film a little less and make me especially nervous for the film that, as a Doom fan, should leave me feeling excited but is instead making me feel the complete opposite way. All I ask for is a faithful adaptation of Dr. Doom in some facet, and I can die happy.

Siguiente paso en la maratón Marvelita para estar un poco al día pre-Spiderman. Bastante sorprendido con que así sea el clímax final de 22 películas, porque realmente Infinity War sí se siente como tal y Endgame solo cumple la última hora y quizá en su planteamiento inicial. El histórico final de la anterior continua con un mundo casi post apocalíptico que me hubiera encantado que se explotara un pelín más. Tras ese inicio, la película claramente tiene el objetivo de llegar a una batalla final épica y falla clamorosamente en la manera de lograrlo. El planteamiento argumental es hacer viajes en el tiempo para robar las gemas del infinito, usarlas para revivir a todo el mundo y devolverlas a su lugar correspondiente para no generar líneas temporales caóticas. A las paradojas propias de las pelis de viajes en el tiempo no se le presta excesiva atención porque tampoco es el sitio, y así se permiten darle alguna patadita a la lógica. Eso funciona como excusa para hacer una especie de repaso a algunas pelis y personajes que se siente un poco liosa, anti climática y de una autorreferencialidad  que juega en contra de la épica de la peli. Esa vuelta a espacios de pelis anteriores sirve como excusa para traer a Thanos (el de la línea temporal actual está muerto) de vuelta, mucho menos desarrollado e interesante que la anterior. Además, lo más grave, es poco consistente con lo ocurrido ya que el personaje parece reaccionar a cosas que él no ha vivido. Por ejemplo, critica a los humanos por no haber sabido aprovechar su plan y por ello los condena a desaparecer para crear un nuevo mundo de cero. No queda natural y parece mucho más villano básico que en la anterior. La última hora vuelve a ser increíble, la batalla final es espectacular y el final con el sacrificio de Iron Man (que inició el MCU y acabó con él hasta ese momento) es muy emotivo.

After being completely blown away by Infinity War , I have to say I’ve been left feeling a little bit disappointed in the saga’s conclusion. Infinity War is very well structured and executes all the beats it needs to hit to deliver something I felt was original and emotionally satisfying. Half of the universe’s population is gone, along with half of the heroes we love, and we’re left feeling hopeless, just like them. This is something we carry with us into the first 30 minutes of Endgame , which again subverted my expectations (positively) and dug the hole of wondering how they’d resolve this even deeper. When then, probably not even 10 minutes later, fucking time travel is thrown out there, it feels incredibly cheap. Instead of carrying the great momentum from the previous film, it becomes, from then on, a kids’ movie. Instead of the events leading the story, which I think made Infinity War so refreshing, it feels predictable, like the events are just following a path that will ultimately end in Marvel getting that big ensemble battle scene they wanted. From the moment time travel was mentioned, all the stakes disappeared. Though I don’t think it was done terribly, and it sets up the multiverse stuff in a good manner. Big spoilers if you somehow don’t know this, but Iron Man’s death hit me way less than I thought it would. Maybe it’s because I already knew it would happen. Maybe it’s because I didn’t watch every Iron Man film in theaters since they first started coming out. But still, I feel like a well-executed death should still do more for me emotionally, especially for a character of such significance. I think, along with a lot of what happens in this film, it was rushed. Yes, it had been foreshadowed—well, at that—but to me it felt like Marvel just thought, «Well, someone has to die. Who would make the most people cry?» And because it’s Iron Man, and Iron Man is Robert Downey Jr., they can just bring him back anyway, and people will eat it up. I don’t like what they did with Thor either. That is not the same fucking guy we saw being willing to give everything to save Asgard. I think Marvel dug themselves into a hole they hadn’t planned a way to get out of, which in the end makes for an overstuffed and rushed saga finale. Like Infinity War , it’s not particularly pretty to look at either, but now without the storytelling chops to make me look past most of it. I think it WOULD be a good film if it were written with a little more thought. Dangerously close to giving this 3 stars. It could easily be split into two films, honestly. It’s 5am now. "There was an idea, Stark knows this, called the Avengers Initiative. The idea was to bring together a group of remarkable people, see if they could become something more. See if they could work together when we needed them to fight the battles we never could." Sam Jackson's Nick Fury hit us with that way back in 2012's The Avengers. At the time, that movie seemed to be the fulfillment of the promise of a shared universe. It was groundbreaking in its own right and was proof that this could actually work. What resulted was a seismic shift in how studios approached making money. All of a sudden, setting up things to come became more important than the film itself and Marvel was no less guilty in said predisposition. It seemed like Kevin Feige's all-pervading control over every aspect of every film would, ultimately, lead to the death of the MCU. Somehow, it didn't. Audiences (me included) flocked in droves to watch the same movie (albeit with different characters and plot) over and over again. We sat through some real abysmal shit too. The "Marvel Formula", however, did not change much. My main issue was always how the film you were watching was always indebted to the next film in the pipeline to fulfill its promises. It seemed like a cycle that would never stop (and probably won't) but then, I watched Endgame. After the "space trash" (to quote David Ehrlich) that we all know as Avengers: Infinity War, Endgame really knocks it out of the park. For once, something had real consequences in the MCU. The sense of loss and grief is palpable. Don't get me wrong, this also a hodgepodge of random character moments structured around a plot that, if you think about it long enough, makes absolutely no sense but what happens to be Endgame's biggest weakness is also its biggest strength. This mish-mash works because its a mish-mash of much fewer characters. They have, and I can't stress this enough, time. The editing, while much tighter than Infinity War's, holds shots much longer than one would expect from a summer blockbuster studio tentpole and this is why, for once, I cried (more than once) in a Marvel film. Imagine the scene where Peter Parker turns into vacuum cleaner food in Tony's hands. Now imagine if an entire 3 hour film was like that. There is one cut that's absolutely ridiculous and doesn't work at all but it'll probably go unnoticed by the majority (pretty much everyone) of the people that watch this film. As you've probably read in other reviews, “fan service” is a huge part of the film. While that isn’t untrue, I prefer to think of these moments as homages and also, the fulfillment of character arcs and sub-arcs. Despite being 3 hours long, there’s very little to the film that I would call unnecessary. It’s almost as if Feige’s plan was to feed us a staple diet of horseshit (no disrespect to the artists that made those films but they were always tied down by the involvement of Feige and, sometimes, the military) for 11 years so that, when they finally did make a great film, we’d know it. And they have. Additionally, both Alan Silvestri’s score and Trent Opaloch’s cinematography happen to be, at least in my opinion, the best in the MCU. Here, Silvestri, unlike in Infinity War, creates a soundscape that builds upon previously established character themes satisfyingly while introducing new, moodier and much more effective pieces into the mix. He no longer has the burden of scoring for Thanos in almost every scene owing to the fact that this film is more The Avengers than The Avengers. A stride was also made towards embracing Joss Whedon’s influence and that pays off in heaps. The lighting gets a little experimental at times and you can see Opaloch’s Disrict 9 come through a little which is honestly great. The CGI is, well, Marvel CGI; rushed, everywhere, and, at this point, it seems like most major studios have stopped caring about the fact that CGI isn’t supposed to look computer generated in almost every case. Despite all its shortcomings, I laughed, I cried, and, on more occasions than I would like to admit, I got goosebumps. This was the endgame all along and it was worth it. If Infinity War was, as @kernetcetera so eloquently described, ‘television’, then Endgame is the TV finale, the send-off show, the goodbye episode that wraps it all up with a nice little bow and gives the fans an opportunity to pay their respects to characters that had been a part of their lives for so many seasons. On that note, it’s certainly not the type of film that was made for someone like me, and I was a fool for thinking it may otherwise have been. I have highlighted my preference for the more singularly focussed storylines in the MCU within previous reviews, with IW being somewhat of an exception. Infinity War surprised me with its acute balance of multiple character threads and plot lines with the fast-paced and action-packed spectacle of superhero powers punching up against the Mad Titan, Thanos. It felt lean and muscly, where the added padding and lethargic pace of Endgame serves as a complete, and for me, unwelcome juxtaposition to what had preceded it. This, admittedly, is down to personal preference. I had wretchedly hoped for an escalation of the Infinity War saga, and was instead handed exactly what franchise fans had asked for all along. Endgame is fan-service through and through, and I have no doubt that day one MCU faithfuls will be absolutely delighted with what’s served up. Where I see po-faced and heavy-handed self-importance, Marvel’s fanbase will instead see earnest and earned tributes to the characters they love and themselves as supporters. And you know what? We’re both right. We’re just coming at it from different directions. If you’re like me, someone who is far more interested in self-contained stories that can stand on their own two feet and are concerned about only what is delivered within a film’s runtime, not what’s outside of it... you’ll probably walk away feeling a little ripped off. If, however, you have completely invested yourself in the 10 years worth of movies that the Marvel Cinematic Universe consists of, you’re unlikely to be disappointed. Enjoy it.

„that is americas ass!“ Edit: So, here is my attempt on writing a proper review explaining my feelings for this movie. Yesterday, when I told one of my “““friends“““" that Avengers: Endgame didn’t blow my mind, that specific someone started insulting one of my favorite movies, La La Land, as „shitty arthouse rom-com“, so I am preparing myself to get hurt again after publishing this. But please leave La La Land out of this, guys. First of all: two stars is not a bad rating. It is slightly lower-than-average. Nothing more or less. Second of all: I haven’t seen every single movie leading up to this one. I would say that I’ve seen all the ones that are really necessary, but I definitely missed some along the way. So, one could argue that I am not as emotionally involved into the storyline as the specific target audience. Now that all of that’s said, lets get into it. Disclaimer: Spoilers! Avengers: Endgame starts off very weird. We get to see what happened after Avengers: Infinity War. Our heroes travel to a distant planet that Thanos is hiding on to get the stones back and to make everything undone. As they find out that the stones have been destroyed, they kill Thanos and return to earth. A, in my opinion, very bumpy beginning. The first 30 minutes just seem very unstructured and repetitious. Maybe they should have ended Infinity War with Thanos destroying the stones and getting killed instead of starting Endgame with that. Or maybe don’t show it at all. Endgame could have startet with Scott coming back from the particle world. He walks around the town just like he really does, sees all those weird monuments, and then goes on to the head quarter. That is where Steve explains what has been going on and that Scott has been missing for 5 years. Scott could be all like „What? That can’t be right! I’ve only been gone for like 5 hours!“ and they figure out this whole time-travelling thing together. That way you safe the shitty „5 years later“-card, 15 minutes of explaining how humanity has been doing these last years, and the incredibly long introduction. And can we please take a moment to talk about how a rat (????) is the reason that Scott comes back in the first place? I can’t possibly believe that this is the best thing they could come up with. How about one of the Avengers, possibly Natasha, still can’t let go and is searching for every clue she can find. Maybe she could be the one saving Scott? I don’t know if that would be any better, I just can’t believe that they are putting humanity’s fate in the hands (or paws?) of a rat. But that is not the only thing that seemed a little dubious to me. There are many things happening that don’t seem to have an real impact on the story. For example: Thanos dies, but the second Thanos from the past just travels to the future to take his place. The head quarter is being blown up, but still nobody gets hurt. The Avengers seem to be losing the war, but Captain Marvel is right around the corner to save their asses. Thanos manages to get the gold glove, but the stones have already been removed. And those are just a few examples. I mean, I know that those are the plot twist that everyone loves so much, but they just didn’t work for me. Making something like this one or two times would have been fine, but they pulled this „something-happens-but-not-really-because-tada-surprise!“-card so many times that i just couldn’t take anything that was happening in the movie seriously. It was just too much for me. But, as one might expect, not only those puns were a bit over-the-top, but also everything else in this movie. I know that this is supposedly the most epic movie in human history, and that if any movie would have the allowance to go all the way it would be this one, but guys…. too much is too much. Every single sentence was implemented as the most dramatic thing that has ever been said. Everyone knows that I love myself a good dramatic scene, but a slow-mo zoom to the person talking ahead of every sentence is a bit exaggerated even for my taste. I know that this film serves the sole purpose of making the fans cry tears of joy and anger, but that is no excuse for the level of epical slow-mos featured in this film. Especially scenes that would have been sad on their own like Tonys funeral are being destroyed for me because of the dolly shot through the crying crowd. I don’t need to see those crying faces to understand the impact of this scene. It is just a pointless way of saying: „Look, that guy’s also there! Do you see this one??? It’s your childhood hero crying! Hah!“. Yes, i get that this is the end of an era and that the fans deserve a way to say goodbye, but the films quality massively suffered due to scenes like this in my opinion. Yes, it was very sad and all, but still not needed to get the message across. I know, it sounds like i am only seeing the bad sides again. But it’s not like that. I actually really liked the framework plot of time travel. That was a solid foundation and executed nicely. The thing that bothered me is that instead of making this movie stand for its own and create something new and inspiring, it seems like it was just created to be closing ceremony for the fans that stuck around the past 11 years. If that is what you are looking for in a film, fine. I accept that, and I am definitely not judging anyone for rating this with 5 stars. It is just not what i had hoped to see. I would have needed something a little more demanding and challenging, not something that is only mend to satisfy my need of a happy ending to this long story. And before you say it, yes, i know that this movie is not meant to stand alone and that it is the product of 11 years of build-up. But more than that, it is also one of the movies with the highest budgets for story development, a huge milestone in film history and a one-of-a-kind crossover that has never been there before. And from a movie like that I would have expected a lot more than „just“ a long and bumpy farewell from my generations heroes. I’m really sorry if my opinion upsets you, but that is just the way I see it. As I said, two stars is not a bad rating. Is a little below average, and that is really that way I am feeling about this movie. So no, this is not a „i hate this because everyone loves it“ kind of thing, this is just my honest opinion. And if you don’t like it, please let me know why. I’m open for discussion. But please don’t hurt my baby La La Land. Second Edit: Now, a few days later, I just have to admit that they almost had me crying in the end. I can’t help it, I am a sucker for love and nothing gets me like reunited lovers do. I am weak.

Bevor ich heute ins Kino ging, hab ich mir noch mal meine „Avengers: Infinity War“-Kritik durchgelesen, um mir all die tollen Aspekte des ersten Teils in Erinnerung zu rufen. Wie ich davon schwärmte, dass die Russo-Brüder mit fast unglaublicher Präzision unzählige Handlungsstränge gekonnt verwoben. Wie ein Studio, das nicht gerade für denkwürdige Antagonisten bekannt ist, urplötzlich einen der brillantesten Bösewichte der Blockbustergeschichte aus dem Ärmel schüttelt. Und wie sich zwischen all dem Getöse immer die richtige Mischung aus emotionalem Unterbau und Spektakel fand. Und jetzt, nach einem Jahr ausharren, zahllosen Theorie-Videos auf Youtube und großen Hoffnungen, kann ich nun sagen: All das, was ich an Infinity War geliebt hatte, ist Endgame…nicht. Verglichen mit dem grandiosen Vorgänger ist das hier nicht nur der deutlich schlechtere Film, sondern eine grandiose Enttäuschung. Ich muss gestehen – ich bin tatsächlich ernsthaft frustriert, dass es gerade mal einen weiteren Teil gebraucht hat und all die guten Ansätze des Vorgängers sind wieder völlig über Bord gegangen. Plötzlich ist Thanos wieder der eindimensionale Tunichtgut, der ab und zu mal im Hintergrund vor sich her grummelt – mehr Tiefe oder Entwicklung gibt es für den Titanen nicht mehr. Klar, der hatte seine Momente dafür im Vorgänger, der seinen Charakter-Arc ziemlich klar zu Ende führte, aber „Endgame“ müsste wie auch schon „Infinity War“ trotzdem für sich genommen funktionieren. Weil hier aber noch mehr als dort viel Vorwissen vorausgesetzt wird und man sich Charaktermotivationen offenbar aus den vorigen Filmen selbstständig zusammendenken muss, wirkt „Endgame“ nie wie ein in sich geschlossener Film, sondern ein Bilderband aus 10 Jahren Marvel-Kino. Und weil Marvel es mit dem Slogan „das epische Finale einer zehnjährigen Reise“ wirklich, WIRKLICH ernst meint, ist das hier mehr ein Abhaken sämtlicher Fanservice-Checkboxen, statt eines kohärenten Einzelwerks. Wie einmal im Schnellverfahren durchs Poesiealbum blättern wirkt das, jeder Charakter bekommt seinen eigenen, speziellen Moment, manchmal um mit vergangenen Dämonen abzuschließen, manchmal um den Fans nochmal zu zeigen „Guck mal, die Figur haben wir auch nicht vergessen.“ Abstruserweise kommt das Pacing in diesen Momenten beinahe zum Erliegen, während der Film andernorts viel zu gehetzt wirkt. Da findet Tony Stark tatsächlich innerhalb einer einzigen Szene mal eben die Formel, für eine der weltbewegendsten Entdeckungen der Menscheitsgeschichte, Ant-Man entkommt aus einer Misere, weil ein Nagetier zufällig über die Apparatur schlendert und die Frage, wie Stark nun überhaupt zur Erde zurückkehrt, wird durch banalste Plotconvenience "beantwortet". Im harten Kontrast dazu stehen viele Dialog- oder Monologsequenzen, die unnötig ausgewalzt werden. Wer den redundanten Motivationsphrasen aus den Trailern noch nicht überdrüssig ist, darf sich auf volle drei Stunden weitere „Egal was es kostet“-Tiraden einstellen. Was mich dabei vor allem schockiert ist, wie sehr dieser Film konzeptionell aus der Rolle fällt. Vielleicht vor allem deshalb, weil „Infinity War“ zuvor so anders war, als der übliche Marvel-Einheitsbrei und „Endgame“ nun genau dort wieder angelangt ist. Es wirkt beinahe, als hätten die Russo Brüder für „Infinity War“ all ihr Feuer verpulvert und würden nun wahllos drauflos filmen. Tonal ist das hier zB völlig uneben. Zu Beginn quälend langatmige Trauerbewältigung, wird „Endgame“ dann zur Mitte plötzlich zum Kindergarten. Ein Schenkelklopfer jagt hier den nächsten, Slapstick-Momente, kesse Oneliner, nahezu keiner davon wirklich clever oder der allgemeinen Grundstimmung entsprechend angebracht. Und - bei allem was heilig ist - was die Russos hier mit Thor veranstalten, grenzt an Heldenschändung – ich hab mich lange nicht mehr so für eine Figur und ihren Darsteller fremdgeschämt. Überhaupt will den Brüder dieses Mal kaum etwas vernünftig gelingen. Derart drastische Logiklöcher (wieso kann eigentlich plötzlich jeder, wie er lustig ist, die Infinitysteine anfassen?) gab es so im Vorgänger nicht. Und der Mittelteil, den die Russos als „Heist Movie“ verkaufen wollen, dabei aber nicht im Ansatz verstanden zu haben scheinen, was einen guten Heist-Film ausmacht, hat mich beinahe eingeschläfert Das plumpe Umhergespringe zwischen den Örtlichkeiten des Marveluniversums lässt weder das perfekte Timing, noch die Spannung der großen Heist-Klassiker erkennen. Man muss aber auch sagen: das hier fühlt sich immerhin wirklich wie ein episches Finale an. Einige Türen werden geschlossen, andere leicht offen gehalten, vor allem im großen Finale (das praktisch im Alleingang die Wertung noch im positiven Rahmen hält) wird es dann noch einmal richtig episch. Die erste Riege der Avengers bekommt hier zumindest auf den letzten Metern ein „Farewell“, das mehr als angemessen ist. Einige Momente werden die Langzeitfans in völlige Ekstase versetzen, andere nachhaltig schockieren. Und klar, auch ich komme da nicht umhin, anzuerkennen was diese Filme, dieses Universum bis hierhin erreicht haben. Ich wünschte nur, die Marvel-Filme würden, wie nun leider auch „Endgame“, nicht immer nur von Moment zu Moment funktionieren, sondern auch mal wieder komplette, vollwertige Filme hervorbringen. „Infinity War“ war so ein Werk – mutig, clever erdacht und mit versierter Hand inszeniert. „Endgame“ ist, obgleich er die Fans wohl mit dem Ende zufrieden stellen wird, rein filmisch nur ein Schatten dieser Glanzleistung. Die Frage, die für mich bleibt ist: ist das jetzt nur ein magerer Abschluss oder ein trauriger Blick in eine Zukunft, voll mit weiterem Marvel-Mittelmaß?

Infierno en el espectáculo más grande sobre la Tierra Una de las películas más taquilleras de 1974 fue The Towering Inferno : un drama de cine catástrofe (y un poco catastrófico) cuyo título resume todo el argumento. En la tradición de The Greatest Show On Earth , The Towering Inferno es un desfile de cameos de actores famosos y dinero: todo es un aparato que fue acompañado por récords en ventas de entradas y hasta nominaciones al Oscar. Pero, pese a tantas entradas vendidas y noninaciones, ambas son películas que parecen haber sido relegadas al olvido hoy en día. El espectáculo (que se traduce en un juego de identificar los segundos de caras famosas cuando aparecen) se opone a la narración: hoy puede resultar más épico sobrevivir a las 3 horas de duración de cada uno de estos títulos que los desafíos que sus respectivos personajes enfrentan. El problema no es el "qué": es el "cómo" se muestra lo que se cuenta. Avengers: Endgame sufre un problema similar. No se trata de cuestionar decisiones argumentales. Hay una idea vertebral dando vueltas que recorre los laberintos del tiempo: ahí es cuando la película se vuelve más interesante. Cuando se aleja de los guiños para fanáticos que establecieron un contrato de lectura previo y de los planos generales de ejércitos incomprensibles sobre un fondo gris, cuando se centra más en los conflictos de los personajes que en las piruetas de héroes, sin peso ni alma, hechos por computadora. El pasado no se olvida pero tampoco puede repetirse: el Capitán América dice "we move forward". Hay una contradicción ontológica dentro de esa misma propuesta que funciona como espejo de las teorías de la imagen tiempo. Pero todo amenaza con diluirse en cameos y malabares logísticos (que tienen que ver más con los nombres que aparecen en pantalla que en innovaciones visuales o estéticas) para cerrar una historia que, con más torpezas que aciertos narrativos, lleva más de una década. La primera unión de los Avengers en la película de Joss Whedon conserva su energía: era la primera vez y estaba claro. Cada vez que se intentó replicar ese "momento" parecía perder más fuerza en la pantalla, aunque el leitmotiv sonara más alto y se amontonaran más y más personajes. A veces menos es más. La cacofonía visual no es sinónimo de emoción y lo que alguna vez fue novedoso ya se convirtió en rutinario. A esta altura uno puede identificar una estructura narrativa definida que incluye referencias pop (en especial, de la década del '80) y algún chiste inocente que contrasta con añadidos serios y dramáticos subrayados por música y encuadres solemnes que desentonan con el espíritu que los precedía. Más triste es que algunos personajes queden relegados a ser un Deus ex machina y que parezcan la representación simbólica no irónica del famoso "debo irme, mi planeta me necesita" de Los Simpson . ¿Por qué forzar personajes interesantes a estar solo para la foto cuando podían ocupar roles más interesantes? Son decisiones artísticas, y algunos no tendrán problema con ellas, pero Endgame no tiene la cohesión narrativa de historias corales tipo Nashville , City Of Angels o Magnolia , aunque lo intenta y eso no es un detalle menor. Infinity War funcionaba porque entendía que los héroes se definen en acciones antes que en palabras. A las piñas: como también sucedía en The Avengers . Tenía un personaje con un arco dramático definido y dividía el tercer acto en tres espacios distintos para darle lugar a cada línea dramática. El montaje en paralelo estaba justificado y adquiría sentido de urgencia. Ni el villano quedaba diluido en el medio del caos ni los héroes se amontonaban. Si todo es épico, nada es épico. Pasaron apenas diez años pero el cine de superhéroes se convirtió en algo tan despersonalizado y homogeneo que, en contraste, películas de estudio como Iron Man , The Dark Knight , Watchmen o Hellboy II muchos las reconocen ahora como productos artesanales que tenían algo para decir sobre el estado del arte y del mundo. Quizás todo se vuelva tan prefabricado y difícil de diferenciar que digamos lo mismo de Endgame en 10 años.

↓ English version below ↓ Alles muss zu einem Abschluss kommen. Und auch wenn das MCU an sich natürlich weiter gehen wird, neigt sich eine Ära dem Ende zu. Zehn Jahre Filmuniversum münden gemeinsam in einem bombastischen, dreistündigen Werk. Endgame greift dabei zunächst den düsteren Ton auf, den Infinity War gelegt hat. Geliebte Menschen und Freunde sind fort. Wut hat sich ebenso wie Trauer und Verzweiflung in den übrig gebliebenen Charakteren angestaut. Es gilt neue Kraft zu schöpfen für ein letztes Aufbäumen. Und was aus Prinzip schon episch und als logische Konsequenz folgen müsste, wird durch reichlich holprige Erzählweise überrumpelt. Endgame springt sowohl in seiner Tonalität, als auch zwischen Schauplätzen hin und her wie ein wild gewordener Flummi. Im einen Moment soll Unheil, Frustration und Leere vorherrschen, nur um wenige Minuten später in kessen One-Linern und stumpfen Slapstick-Gags zu versinken. Und dabei ist der Humor nicht mal schlecht, er will nur gar nicht in dieses schwere, emotionale Biest von Film hinein passen. Infinity War hat das dosierter und punktuierter hin bekommen, ohne die Atmosphäre zu brechen. Im Endgame gelingt das nicht. Hier werden ganze Figuren kurzer Hand zum Running-Gag umgeschrieben, der sich selbst bis zur letzten Szene vor den Credits aufrecht hält. Der Ausgleich zwischen ruhigen Momenten und Action funktioniert hingegen gut und es wird sich Zeit für Exposition und Charakterentwicklung genommen, wenn auch nicht immer in den passendsten Momenten. Eine rührende Reunion mitten auf einem riesigen, tobenden Schlachtfeld ist alles andere als von Logik geprägt. Ähnlich staunt man, wenn der Film im Mittelteil mir nichts dir nichts ein Heist-Kapitel aus dem Hut zaubert, welches das Tempo nochmal komplett umkrempelt. Handwerklich zwar von Größen des Genres entfernt, macht die Idee aber immerhin Spaß und sorgt für Abwechslung während den 180 Minuten Laufzeit, die sich tatsächlich aber nicht danach anfühlen. Dafür passiert insgesamt zu viel, Details wollen erkannt und Schlüsse gezogen werden. Und auch wenn das funktioniert, fühlt es sich erneut wie eine Schablone an, die mit wenigen Ausahmen niemals ausbricht. Diesen winzigen, aber wichtigen Schritt nach vorn, der mit Infinity War gesetzt wurde, geht man hier zurück und liefert die immer gleichen Marotten, wie in den vergangenen zehn Jahren. Damit spielt man ganz zielsicher den Fan-Herzen in die Arme und es fehlt an nichts für einen soliden MCU-Beitrag, aber wenn man es sich getraut hätte noch einen Schritt nach vorne zu machen, hätte man zum Abschluss vielleicht nochmal alle überrascht - selbst die an die Schablone gewöhnten Fans. Endgame fühlt sich an, als ob Opa Marvel vom Krieg erzählt. Man blättert durch alte Geschichten und besinnt sich auf Vergangenes zurück. Doch dieser Krieg ist gerade mal zehn Jahre her und wir haben ihn live miterlebt und man kann Opas alte Leier nicht mehr hören. Und trotz oder eben gerade aufgrund der Gewöhnung werden treu ergebene MCU-Fans dieses Endgame mögen. Vielleicht sogar lieben. Die Verbundenheit zu über die Jahre ans Herz gewachsenen Charakteren, über viele Filme aufgebaute Beziehungen, Meinungsverschiedenheiten, Rivalitäten - alles mündet in diesen 180 Minuten. Wer sich in den letzten zehn Jahren auf eine emotionale Reise durch dieses Franchise mitnehmen hat lassen, wird im Endgame jubeln, weinen und schreien. Für jene, werden dies die schönsten und zeitgleich schlimmsten drei Stunden des Kinojahres. Wer das alles nicht von sich behaupten kann, bekommt immer noch einen soliden Action-Blockbuster, in dem mehr steckt, als man ihm zutraut, der aber nie das Potential entfacht, das in ihm lodert. --------------------------------------------------------------- Everything has to come to a conclusion. And even though the MCU itself will of course continue, an era is drawing to a close. Ten years of the film universe lead together to a bombastic, three-hour work. Endgame first picks up the dark tone Infinity War has set. Beloved people and friends are gone. Anger has accumulated in the remaining characters as well as sadness and despair. There is new strength to draw for a last rebellion. And what should follow epically and as a logical consequence is taken by surprise by a bumpy narrative. Endgame jumps back and forth in its tonality as well as between locations like a wild bouncy ball. In one moment disaster, frustration and emptiness should prevail, only to sink a few minutes later into cheeky one-liners and blunt slapstick gags. And the humor isn't even bad, it just doesn't want to fit into this heavy, emotional beast of film. Infinity War has managed to do this in a dosed and punctual way, without breaking the atmosphere. In the endgame this isn't possible. Here whole characters are rewritten into a running gag, which keeps itself upright until the last scene before the credits. The balance between quiet moments and action works well and time is taken for exposure and character development, even if not always in the most appropriate moments. A touching reunion in the middle of a huge, raging battlefield is anything but logical. Similarly, you're astonished when the movie in the middle section doesn't conjure up a hot chapter out of your hat, which completely changes the tempo again. Although it's far removed from the genre's greats in terms of craftsmanship, the idea is at least fun and provides variety during the 180 minutes of running time, which actually don't feel like it. Too much happens, details have to be recognized and conclusions have to be drawn. And even if that works, it feels like a template again that never breaks out with a few exceptions. This tiny, but important step forward that was made with Infinity War is taken back here and you always get the same fads as in the past ten years. It's a sure-fire way to play into the hearts of fans and there's nothing missing for a solid MCU contribution, but if you dared to take another step forward, you might have surprised everyone at the end - even the fans used to the stencil. Endgame feels like Grandpa Marvel's telling about the war. One leafs through old stories and recalls the past. But this war was only ten years ago and we experienced it live and you can't hear Grandpa's old lyre anymore. And despite or just because of the habituation loyal MCU fans will like this Endgame. Maybe even love it. The connection to characters that have grown to heart over the years, relationships built up through many films, differences of opinion, rivalries - everything ends in these 180 minutes. Anyone who has been taken on an emotional journey through this franchise in the last ten years will cheer, cry and scream in the Endgame. For those of you, this will be the most beautiful and at the same time the worst three hours of the cinematic year. If you can't claim all this for yourself, you'll still get a solid action blockbuster that contains more than you'd expect, but never unleashes the potential that blazes in it.

Auch wenn Kevin Feige erst kürzlich bekannt gab, dass Avengers: Endgame nicht das Ende der dritten Phase im Marvel Cinematic Universe darstellt, sondern der Abschluss erst mit Spider-Man: Far From Home erfolgt, so werden viele Fans die meisten ihrer Helden, zumindest vereint, ein letztes mal auf der großen Leinwand zu Gesicht bekommen. Nach 11 Jahren und (inklusive Endgame) 22 Filmen neigt sich die bislang größte Superhelden Ära mit dem MCU dem Ende entgegen. Zugegebenermaßen war ich vor dem Kinobesuch auch nervöser als dies für gewöhnlich der Fall ist. Denn unabhängig davon wie es den Russo Brüdern wohl gelingen würde einen Abschluss zu finden, war schon im Vorfeld sicher das ein solches Epos mit Wahnsinnscast und vielen liebgewonnenen Charakteren so schnell nicht wieder im Kino zu finden sein wird. Viele Filmemacher wären dankbar auch nur einer Bruchteil des Endgame Casts in ihren Werken inszenieren zu dürfen. Selbst in den Nebenrollen findet sich kaum mehr ein Name der nicht bereits zu der Elite Hollywoods zählt. Doch hier geht Avengers: Endgame endlich den nötigen Schritt weiter und gibt vielen Charakteren, für eine Superheldenverfilmung ungewöhnlich viel Möglichkeit wahre Schauspielkunst darzubieten und starke Emotionen abzuliefern. Passenderweise entfaltet im direkten Anschluss an die Geschehnissen aus Avengers: Infinity War, gerade die Eröffnungssequenz einen ungewöhnlichen, schon fast traurigen Tiefgang, welcher bislang im MCU nur selten auch nur im Ansatz so zu finden war. Generell hat man sich für den Auftakt etwas spezielles einfallen lassen und hebt sich bereits hier von allen anderen MCU Filmen etwas ab. Bedingt durch die gut bemessene Laufzeit von 181 Minuten schafft es Avengers: Endgame wie auch schon sein direkter Vorgänger auf beeindruckende Weise alles unter einen Hut zu bekommen. So hat man nie das Gefühl das sich die Macher in gewissen Szenen abhetzen mussten, oder gar aus Budgetgründen auf gewisse Ereignisse lieber verzichtet werden musste. Einigen Superhelden-Fans, den Origin Storys aufgrund der meist weniger stattfindenden Actionszenen zu schwerfällig bzw. träge sind, wird Avengers: Endgame im zweiten und dritten Viertel womöglich etwas zu wenig brachiale Action-Spektakel bieten. Gerade da Avengers: Infinity War für mein empfinden den ausgewogeneren Mix aus Story und Action geboten hat. Insgesamt lassen sich weniger Highlights finden die das geneigte Kamp Choreo Herz höher schlagen lassen. Dennoch gibt es genügend spektakulär inszenierte Fights und gigantische Zerstörungsorgien die sich allesamt von der visuellen Umsetzung her mehr als sehen lassen können. Wie Eingangs erwähnt bekommen einige Charaktere mehr Entfaltungsspielraum und können zeigen das sie nicht nur Superhelden sind, sonder hinter der Maske doch nur "Menschen" stecken. Um in keiner Weise auch nur den kleinsten Spoiler zu liefern, halte ich es an dieser Stelle sehr Wage und gehe nicht auf die einzelnen Leistungen der Darsteller ein. Nur so viel sei gesagt, allesamt legen die Messlatte sehr hoch und liefern somit den emotionalsten aller Superheldenfilme ab. Der Score ist äußerst passend gewählt und bietet eine extrem große Bandbreite für das vorliegende Wechselbad der Gefühle und die gezeigten Geschehnisse. Die Kameraarbeit ist natürlich on Point und vereint von allen bisher speziell für Marvel Filme genutzten Einstellungen nur das beste. Fazit Mit Avengers: Endgame findet das bisher größte Franchise das je in den Kinosälen zu finden war einen würdigen Abschluss. Kein Ereignis kommt zu kurz und dennoch wird der Film die Lager spalten. Es wird viele Stimmen geben die Kritik üben werden und gerade den Fanservice im letzen Akt als unangebracht verurteilen. Ich für meinen Teil kann mit dem Endprodukt sehr gut Leben und habe nur wenig auszusetzen.

READ THE REVIEW IN FULL HERE Eleven years in the making, Avengers: Endgame is the finale to Marvel’s epic cinematic universe, one which has consistently broken box office records and won vast critical praise, combining its blockbuster might with the delicate storytelling and sociocultural consciousness of auteur-led cinema. It is unequivocally the series’ crowning achievement. It’s been twenty-one days since Thanos snapped his infinity gauntlet-clad fingers, evaporating half of all living beings to ash. Such massive existential trauma lays the groundwork for an initially sombre tone, the Avengers wallowing in despair. But once the tragic effects of Avengers: Infinity War have been explored, Endgame establishes its own story, one appropriately saturated with action set-pieces while never ignoring vital and deep character development. Unlike other ensemble pieces within the genre, Christopher Markus and Stephen McFeely’s screenplay is precisely paced. Each character – and there are a lot of them – is given the perfect amount of screen time. Markus and McFeely know exactly where to subvert natural expectations; thus, while plot twists consistently surprise, they never feel shoehorned. And despite the largely existential themes explored – death, sacrifice, individual meaning – they find balance for the trademark quips and signature humour which have come to define the series. The MVP of the ensemble is Robert Downey Jr., who puts in the best performance of his career as Tony Stark, aided by a gorgeous script which gives his stony-faced character an edge of sensitivity, upholding an already cathartic climax. And let’s be clear here: Avengers: Endgame is saturated with catharsis. You’ll come away weeping. Style and content almost perfectly coalesce in Endgame, combining a well-structured narrative and rich characterisation with grand set pieces. This epic close to the biggest cultural phenomenon of our time is a resounding triumph for Kevin Feige, the Russo Brothers, and Marvel Studios. Follow us on Twitter!

As vésperas de completar 11 anos de seu primeiro lançamento, a Marvel Studios finaliza no dia 25 de abril, todos os arcos apresentados ao longo da última década. ‘That's the endgame' Tony Stark previu o título do filme lá em Era de Ultron, se referindo ao perigo que viria do espaço eventualmente. Vingadores Ultimato, título que foi dado no Brasil, vem para quebrar recordes, seja na bilheteria ou no número de pessoas chorando simultaneamente. Um filme que chega com status para se tornar maior de todos os tempos no seu gênero e permanecer nesse patamar por um bom tempo. Ao longo dos quase 11 anos de estúdio, foram 22 filmes, nem todos agradaram o público que é fanático, mas havia uma história maior sendo contada a cada filme. Em Vingadores Ultimato vemos tudo culminar em um filme grandioso, que amarra todas as pontas soltas e usa isso como alavanca para um roteiro excepcionalmente bem escrito. A direção mais uma vez impecável, é como se eu estivesse lendo um quadrinho realmente, a estética ,design de produção e até a fotografia, são retiradas diretamente das páginas. O filme tem um ritmo bom para o número enorme de personagens e para a história que os irmãos Russo querem passar. As cenas de ação são de tirar o folego e te deixar extremamente tenso na poltrona, principalmente a batalha final. As piadas e o clima leve da Marvel estão presentes e dão a quebra necessária de humor para o filme que carrega muita dramaticidade em cada um dos núcleos e personagens da história. Vemos personagens antes coadjuvantes ou que nem deram as caras em Guerra Infinita, agora ganhando seu protagonismo e mais tempo de tela, Scott Lang e Clint Barton são exemplos disso e tem papel fundamental na trama. Nebulosa é uma das estrelas do filme, a complexidade da personagem é mostrada de forma mais ampla e ela se torna o ponto chave para o enredo. Todo mundo tem seu protagonismo, seja ele de forma rápida ou não, todos tem seu tempo para brilhar, o que com certeza traz cenas que levarão os fãs a empolgação máxima na sala de cinema. (GRL PWR representadíssimo em uma cena maravilhosa) Mais uma vez os irmãos Russo entregaram o que prometeram e muito mais, então, melhor se prepararem para sentir um misto de emoções dentro de 3h00m57s que encerram uma era do cinema.
